title: M55, NGC 6809
caption: The globular cluster M55, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: This composite shows M55, also cataloged as NGC 6809, a globular cluster in the constellation Sagittarius. It is fairly large on the sky, spanning about two thirds of the Moon's diameter, but its stars are spread very loosely, giving it an appearance that is barely like a globular cluster at all.
M55 lies about 18000 light-years away and is about 100 light-years across.

A globular cluster is typically a dense, ball-shaped swarm of old stars, packed so tightly toward the center that the core often blurs into a single glow. Clusters vary in how concentrated they are, and loose ones like M55 let telescopes pick out individual stars even near the middle. Because all of a cluster's stars formed at roughly the same time, comparing them helps astronomers work out how stars of different masses age, and globular clusters in particular preserve a record of our Galaxy's distant past.
scale: M55 is about 18000 light-years away and about 100 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: The Burrell Schmidt telescope on Kitt Peak recorded M55 in visible light, combined into a composite. The filters and color mapping are not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather much more light than the eye, resolving many stars across the cluster's loose spread.
